vulnerabilities.name: State-Changing Request Without CSRF Token
vulnerabilities.description: A POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE request that changes state (account settings, password, funds transfer) carries no CSRF token in the body, headers, or a custom per-request value, relying only on session cookies for authentication.
vulnerabilities.notes: Absence of any csrf/xsrf-named header or hidden form field across the captured state-changing requests is the primary indicator; confirm by diffing the request body for a token field.

vulnerabilities.name: CSRF Cookie Missing SameSite Attribute
vulnerabilities.description: Session cookie is issued without SameSite=Lax/Strict (or explicitly SameSite=None without a compensating CSRF token), so the browser will still attach it to cross-site requests originating from another site.
vulnerabilities.notes: SameSite=None is acceptable only when paired with Secure and an independent CSRF-token defense; flag when None appears without a token-based mitigation observed elsewhere in the flow.

vulnerabilities.name: CSRF Token Accepted When Omitted or Blank
vulnerabilities.description: Server-side validation of the CSRF token is not enforced: a state-changing request with the token field removed entirely, or sent as an empty value, is still processed (non-error response).
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by replaying a captured state-changing request with the token header/field stripped and observing a success status rather than 400/403.

vulnerabilities.name: CSRF Token Not Bound to Session (Static or Reusable)
vulnerabilities.description: The anti-CSRF token is identical across sessions, users, or requests (not regenerated per session/request), so a token obtained from one context (e.g. the attacker's own account) can be replayed against the victim.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by comparing the token value across two independent sessions (different cookies jars / incognito) and finding it identical or predictably derived.

vulnerabilities.name: Double-Submit Cookie Without Server-Side Secret Binding
vulnerabilities.description: Server only checks that a request header/body token matches a cookie value (double-submit pattern) without an HMAC or server-side session binding, so an attacker able to set any cookie on their own origin (e.g. via a related subdomain) can also forge the matching header.
vulnerabilities.notes: Higher risk when combined with a permissive cookie scope (Domain=.example.com) letting any subdomain set the comparison cookie.

vulnerabilities.name: State Change via GET Request
vulnerabilities.description: A GET request alone (no body, no custom header) performs a state-changing action, making it trivially forgeable via a plain / tag or 302 redirect with no preflight or SameSite protection applicable to top-level navigation.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed when the same action is normally exposed as GET and succeeds using only the session cookie, with no token parameter required.

vulnerabilities.name: Missing Origin/Referer Validation on State-Changing Requests
vulnerabilities.description: Server does not check the Origin or Referer header on state-changing requests as a secondary defense, so a cross-site forged request succeeds purely on cookie presence.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by replaying a captured request with Origin/Referer altered to an unrelated third-party domain and observing the request still succeeds.

vulnerabilities.name: JSON Content-Type Requirement Bypassed via Form-Encoded Body
vulnerabilities.description: Application relies on requiring Content-Type: application/json as an implicit CSRF defense (since HTML forms cannot natively send it), but the endpoint also accepts application/x-www-form-urlencoded or text/plain for the same action, which a plain HTML form can submit cross-site.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by resending a captured JSON request with the same parameters re-encoded as form-urlencoded/text-plain and the same Content-Type swapped.

vulnerabilities.name: CSRF Token Validated Only Client-Side
vulnerabilities.description: The CSRF token is checked in client-side JavaScript before submission but the server-side endpoint performs no corresponding validation, so a request crafted outside the normal UI flow bypasses the control entirely.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by issuing the state-changing request directly (bypassing the page's JS) with the token omitted and observing success.

vulnerabilities.name: Permissive CORS Enabling Cross-Origin CSRF-Style Reads
vulnerabilities.description: A reflected or wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true lets a malicious page issue authenticated cross-origin requests and read the JSON response, going beyond classic blind CSRF into full response disclosure.
vulnerabilities.notes: Cross-reference with cors_vuln.json — this entry marks where a CORS misconfiguration specifically upgrades CSRF exposure from blind write to readable response.
